stem: A 25-year-old woman has bleeding gums and pinpoint red spots on both shins that appeared two weeks after a head cold. She has never had abnormal bleeding before, takes no medicines and has no liver disease. Her hemoglobin and white cell count are normal.
oneliner: 25F + gum bleeding + petechiae 2 wk after a cold + no prior bleeding + no drugs, no liver disease + normal Hb and WBC → which coagulation set?
ask: Which set of changes best fits her results?

whyNot.A: A normal count with long bleeding time and aPTT fits **von Willebrand disease**, a lifelong disorder; she **never bled before** and the bleeding began after a viral illness
whyNot.B: An isolated long aPTT (factor deficiency) gives deep bleeds into joints and muscle, not **petechiae** and gum bleeding
whyNot.D: Needs **consumption of factors** (e.g. DIC from sepsis or malignancy); she is well, with no liver disease to impair factor synthesis
whyNot.E: Early **vitamin K or warfarin effect** gives a long PT alone; it does not cause petechiae or a low count

answer: Low platelets, long bleeding time, normal PT and aPTT
why: Petechiae and gum bleeding are **primary hemostasis** failure: too few platelets, so the **bleeding time is prolonged**. The coagulation cascade is intact, so **PT and aPTT stay normal**. A viral trigger, isolated thrombocytopenia and otherwise normal counts fit immune thrombocytopenia.
chain: Antibodies coat platelets after a viral illness
Spleen removes them, platelet count falls
Platelet plug forms poorly, bleeding time rises
Clotting factors are untouched, PT and aPTT stay normal

idea.rule: Platelet problems lengthen bleeding time and leave PT and aPTT alone; factor problems do the opposite.
also: Von Willebrand disease: bleeding time up, aPTT normal or up, count normal
Hemophilia A or B: aPTT up, bleeding time and PT normal
Aspirin: bleeding time up, count, PT and aPTT normal
DIC: count down and PT and aPTT both up

stem: A 64-year-old man with chronic pancreatitis and greasy, floating stools for years now bruises easily and his gums bleed when he brushes his teeth. He takes no anticoagulants. Initial testing shows a normal platelet count.
oneliner: 64M + chronic pancreatitis + greasy stools + new bruising and gum bleeding + normal platelets → which coagulation set?
ask: Which set of changes best fits his results?

whyNot.A: An isolated long aPTT suggests an **intrinsic-pathway** defect such as hemophilia; the factors lost here include **factor VII**, which lengthens PT too
whyNot.B: Low platelets and fibrinogen mean **consumption** (DIC); his count is **normal** and nothing suggests a trigger
whyNot.C: Normal clotting times with a low count is a platelet disorder; his **platelet count is normal**
whyNot.D: Bleeding with all tests normal would fit a mild platelet-function or vessel problem; **fat malabsorption** implies factor loss

answer: PT and aPTT both prolonged; platelets and fibrinogen normal
why: Fat malabsorption from pancreatic insufficiency removes **fat-soluble vitamin K**, so factors **II, VII, IX and X** (and proteins C and S) are made without gamma-carboxylation. **PT rises first** because factor VII has the shortest half-life, then **aPTT** follows. Platelets and **fibrinogen are normal** because neither needs vitamin K.
chain: Steatorrhea malabsorbs vitamin K
Factors II, VII, IX, X not carboxylated
Factor VII (shortest half-life) falls first, PT rises
As the other factors fall, aPTT rises too
Platelets and fibrinogen are unaffected

idea.rule: Vitamin K loss lengthens PT first, then aPTT, with normal platelets and fibrinogen.
also: Warfarin: same pattern, PT (INR) rises first
Newborn without prophylaxis: hemorrhagic disease of the newborn
Prolonged broad-spectrum antibiotics reduce gut vitamin K production
Cholestasis or biliary obstruction: bile salts needed to absorb vitamin K

stem: A 30-year-old woman is admitted with fever, low blood pressure and a foul vaginal discharge after an unsafe termination of pregnancy. Blood cultures are drawn. Over the next hours she oozes from the IV sites and from every venipuncture, and the smear shows fragmented red cells.
oneliner: 30F + septic after infected abortion + oozing from IV and puncture sites + fragmented red cells → which coagulation set?
ask: Which set of changes best fits her results?

whyNot.A: A low count alone with normal clotting tests is a primary platelet problem; **oozing from every puncture site** in sepsis means factors are being used up too
whyNot.B: Vitamin K loss lengthens PT and aPTT but forms no fibrin, so it would not give **fragmented red cells** or a low count
whyNot.D: A lone long aPTT (hemophilia) is lifelong and does not cause **fragmented red cells** or new oozing during sepsis
whyNot.E: Fibrinogen is **used up** in DIC, so it falls, and fibrin degradation makes the D-dimer **rise**

answer: PT and aPTT up; platelets and fibrinogen down; D-dimer up
why: Sepsis triggers diffuse **thrombin generation**, forming microthrombi that **consume platelets, clotting factors and fibrinogen**, so PT and aPTT lengthen. Plasmin then breaks down fibrin, raising **D-dimer**, and red cells shear on the fibrin strands to give **schistocytes**.
chain: Sepsis releases tissue factor and cytokines
Widespread thrombin activation, fibrin microthrombi
Platelets, factors and fibrinogen consumed: PT and aPTT up, platelets and fibrinogen down
Plasmin lyses fibrin: D-dimer up
Red cells fragment on fibrin strands: schistocytes

idea.rule: DIC consumes everything: long PT and aPTT, low platelets and fibrinogen, high D-dimer.
also: Amniotic fluid embolism and abruptio placentae
Acute promyelocytic leukemia (t(15;17))
Metastatic adenocarcinoma, especially mucinous
Snake envenomation and massive trauma

stem: A 72-year-old man who has never smoked has a ruddy face and itching after hot showers. Examination shows an enlarged spleen. Pulse oximetry on room air reads 98%. Hemoglobin is 20.5 g/dL, and his white cell and platelet counts are also raised.
oneliner: 72M + never-smoker + ruddy face + itching after hot showers + splenomegaly + SaO2 98% + Hb 20.5 + high WBC and platelets → which set of SaO2, EPO and red cell mass?
ask: Which set of changes best fits his results?

options.A: O2 saturation ↓, erythropoietin ↑, red cell mass ↑
options.B: O2 saturation ↔, erythropoietin ↑, red cell mass ↑
options.C: O2 saturation ↔, erythropoietin ↔, red cell mass ↔
options.D: O2 saturation ↔, erythropoietin ↓, red cell mass ↑
options.E: O2 saturation ↓, erythropoietin ↓, red cell mass ↑

whyNot.A: This is **hypoxia-driven** secondary polycythemia; his saturation is **98%**
whyNot.B: An **EPO-secreting tumor** (e.g. renal cell carcinoma) would raise EPO; it would not explain the raised **white cells, platelets** and splenomegaly
whyNot.C: A **relative** polycythemia from low plasma volume leaves red cell mass normal; it would not raise **white cells and platelets** or enlarge the spleen
whyNot.E: Low saturation would drive EPO **up**; this combination is physiologically inconsistent

answer: Normal saturation, low erythropoietin, raised red cell mass
why: A **JAK2 V617F** mutation makes the marrow proliferate on its own: red cell mass rises along with white cells and platelets. Oxygen saturation is **normal**, and the excess red cells suppress renal **erythropoietin** by negative feedback.
chain: JAK2 V617F drives autonomous marrow growth
Red cell mass (and WBC, platelets) rises
Oxygen delivery is more than adequate, kidney senses no hypoxia
Erythropoietin falls (negative feedback)

idea.rule: Polycythemia vera is the one with high red mass despite normal oxygen and low EPO.
also: Secondary polycythemia from COPD or altitude: low SaO2, high EPO
Renal cell carcinoma or hepatocellular carcinoma: EPO made by the tumor
Dehydration: relative rise only, red cell mass normal
EPO-secreting cerebellar hemangioblastoma (von Hippel-Lindau): EPO high, unlike PV

stem: A 60-year-old man with a 50 pack-year smoking history and a chronic productive cough has bluish lips and a hemoglobin of 18.5 g/dL. His white cell and platelet counts are normal and he has no splenomegaly. Pulse oximetry on room air reads 84%.
oneliner: 60M + 50 pack-years + chronic cough + cyanosis + Hb 18.5 + SaO2 84% + normal WBC and platelets + no splenomegaly → which set of SaO2, EPO and red cell mass?
ask: Which set of changes best fits his results?

options.A: O2 saturation ↓, erythropoietin ↑, red cell mass ↑
options.B: O2 saturation ↔, erythropoietin ↓, red cell mass ↑
options.C: O2 saturation ↔, erythropoietin ↑, red cell mass ↑
options.D: O2 saturation ↔, erythropoietin ↔, red cell mass ↔
options.E: O2 saturation ↓, erythropoietin ↓, red cell mass ↓

whyNot.B: This is a **primary** marrow disorder, and his saturation is clearly **low**
whyNot.C: An EPO-secreting tumor would not lower his saturation to **84%**
whyNot.D: Dehydration gives a relative rise only; his low saturation and long smoking history point to a **true** increase in red mass
whyNot.E: Chronic hypoxia drives EPO **up** and red cell mass **up**, the opposite of this set

answer: Low saturation, high erythropoietin, raised red cell mass
why: Chronic lung disease keeps arterial saturation low. Renal peritubular cells sense the **hypoxia** (HIF-mediated) and increase **erythropoietin**, so only the **red cell line** expands, with normal white cells and platelets and no splenomegaly.
chain: COPD lowers oxygen saturation
Kidney senses hypoxia, EPO rises
Marrow makes more red cells, red mass rises
White cells and platelets unaffected

idea.rule: Hypoxia raises EPO and red cell mass; autonomous polycythemia lowers EPO.
also: High altitude residence
Obstructive sleep apnea or obesity hypoventilation
Cyanotic congenital heart disease
Renal artery stenosis or hydronephrosis: local renal hypoxia raises EPO

stem: A 50-year-old man has 2 months of worsening breathlessness on exertion and fatigue. He looks pale, and his respiratory rate is 22/min. Hemoglobin is 7 g/dL. Arterial PO2 on room air is 96 mm Hg.
oneliner: 50M + exertional dyspnea + pallor + RR 22 + Hb 7 + PaO2 96 → which set of O2 values?
ask: Which set of changes is expected with his underlying problem?

options.A: PaO2 ↓, SaO2 ↓, arterial O2 content ↓, mixed venous PO2 ↓
options.B: PaO2 ↔, SaO2 ↔, arterial O2 content ↓, mixed venous PO2 ↓
options.C: PaO2 ↔, SaO2 ↔, arterial O2 content ↔, mixed venous PO2 ↑
options.D: PaO2 ↔, SaO2 ↓, arterial O2 content ↓, mixed venous PO2 ↓
options.E: PaO2 ↔, SaO2 ↔, arterial O2 content ↑, mixed venous PO2 ↔

whyNot.A: Falling PaO2 and saturation mean a **lung or ventilation** problem; his PaO2 is **96**
whyNot.C: Normal content with a high venous PO2 means tissues **cannot use** oxygen (e.g. cyanide); with **Hb 7** content must be low
whyNot.D: A low saturation with normal PaO2 needs hemoglobin blocked by another ligand; nothing suggests an exposure, and **Hb 7** explains his symptoms
whyNot.E: A high content would need excess hemoglobin; his hemoglobin is **7 g/dL**

answer: Normal PaO2 and saturation, low arterial O2 content, low mixed venous PO2
why: Anemia means too little hemoglobin to carry oxygen, so **content falls** while **PaO2 and saturation stay normal** (dissolved oxygen and percent saturation are unchanged). Tissues still extract their oxygen from a smaller supply, so **mixed venous content and PO2 fall**.
chain: Low hemoglobin concentration
Arterial O2 content falls, PaO2 and SaO2 unchanged
Tissues extract the same amount of oxygen from less
Mixed venous O2 content and PO2 fall
Breathing quickens to compensate for poor delivery

idea.rule: PaO2 reflects dissolved oxygen only; content depends on how much hemoglobin there is and how much of it carries oxygen.
also: Carbon monoxide poisoning: PaO2 normal, true saturation and content low
Methemoglobinemia: PaO2 normal, saturation and content low
Polycythemia: PaO2 normal, content high
High altitude: PaO2 low, so saturation and content fall too

stem: A 10-year-old boy with a very high white cell count starts induction chemotherapy for acute lymphoblastic leukemia. The next day he has flank pain, dark urine and passes little urine. Blood tests are sent.
oneliner: 10M + high-burden leukemia + day 2 of induction chemotherapy + flank pain + dark urine + oliguria → which chemistry set?
ask: Which set of changes best fits his blood tests?

whyNot.A: Dying cells **release** potassium and phosphate, so both rise, and phosphate binds calcium to **lower** it
whyNot.C: Intracellular phosphate and purines are released too: phosphate and uric acid **rise**, and calcium falls
whyNot.D: Three are right; the **calcium rise** is wrong because phosphate precipitates calcium
whyNot.E: An isolated uric acid rise is a **gout** picture; mass cell lysis releases intracellular ions as well

answer: Potassium, phosphate and uric acid up; calcium down
why: Rapid lysis of tumor cells releases **potassium, phosphate and nucleic acids**. Purines are catabolised to **uric acid**, which crystallises in the tubules and causes acute kidney injury. Excess **phosphate binds calcium** (calcium phosphate), so serum calcium falls.
chain: Chemotherapy lyses a large tumor burden
Intracellular K and phosphate released
Nucleic acids broken down to uric acid
Phosphate binds calcium: hypocalcemia
Uric acid and calcium phosphate crystals injure the kidney

idea.rule: Tumor lysis = hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hyperuricemia and hypocalcemia.
also: Burkitt lymphoma and high-count leukemias are classic
Rhabdomyolysis: potassium, phosphate and urate up, calcium down
Bulky tumors can lyse spontaneously before treatment
Crush injury releases muscle cell contents the same way

stem: In an experiment, a volunteer's circulating red cells are tagged with a marker once. No more marker is given afterwards. His spleen and marrow are normal.
oneliner: Experiment: red cells tagged once, no more label, normal spleen and marrow → how long until no tagged cells remain?
ask: About how long before essentially all the tagged cells are gone?

whyNot.A: Far shorter than red cell survival; this is closer to the neutrophil life in blood
whyNot.B: Platelets last about 7 to 10 days; red cells last much longer
whyNot.C: Only a quarter of the true red cell lifespan
whyNot.E: Red cells are not that long-lived; they have no nucleus to repair themselves

why: A normal red cell survives about **120 days**, then macrophages in the **spleen** remove it. A cohort labelled once is therefore fully replaced in **about 4 months**.
chain: Red cells lack nucleus and organelles
Membrane and enzymes wear out over time
Macrophages in the spleen remove old cells at about 120 days
Tagged cohort is gone in about 4 months

idea.rule: Red cell lifespan is about 120 days.
also: Platelets live 7 to 10 days
Neutrophils circulate only hours
HbA1c reflects glucose over the 2-3 month red cell lifespan
Hemolysis shortens red cell survival, so reticulocytes rise

stem: A 17-year-old girl is brought in after a car accident with major blood loss and receives volume resuscitation. Her bone marrow and iron stores are normal. Blood is tested on day 1 and again on day 5.
oneliner: 17F + major hemorrhage after car crash + healthy marrow and iron stores + labs day 1 and day 5 → which set of EPO, reticulocytes and heme synthesis?
ask: Which set of changes best describes the response by day 5?

whyNot.A: The kidney senses reduced oxygen delivery and raises EPO first; reticulocytes cannot rise without it
whyNot.B: EPO stimulates the marrow, so by day 5 with iron and marrow normal, reticulocytes **rise**
whyNot.C: More red cell production needs more heme, so ALA synthase must be **up**
whyNot.D: Low oxygen delivery **stimulates** EPO rather than suppressing it

answer: EPO, reticulocytes and ALA synthase all increased
why: Blood loss reduces oxygen delivery, so renal peritubular cells release **erythropoietin**. The marrow responds over several days with a **reticulocytosis**. Making new hemoglobin needs heme, so **ALA synthase**, the rate-limiting enzyme of heme synthesis, increases.
chain: Hemorrhage lowers oxygen delivery to kidney
Erythropoietin rises within hours
Marrow proliferates and releases reticulocytes after days
Heme demand rises, ALA synthase activity up
Hemoglobin recovers over weeks if iron is available

idea.rule: Acute loss raises EPO at once; reticulocytes follow in days.
also: Hemolysis: EPO up, reticulocytes up within days
Iron replacement for deficiency: reticulocytes peak in about a week
B12 or folate replacement: reticulocytosis within days
High altitude: EPO up within hours, red cell mass over weeks

stem: A 10-month-old boy with sickle cell anemia (HbSS) develops painful swelling of both feet. He has had two days of vomiting and poor oral intake.
oneliner: 10-month-old M + HbSS + painful swollen feet + 2 days vomiting and poor intake → which red cell change promotes sickling?
ask: Which change in his red cells most likely favored the process causing his foot pain?

whyNot.A: HbF **interrupts** HbS polymerization and is protective
whyNot.B: Alkalosis raises oxygen affinity, **reducing** polymerization; acidosis promotes it
whyNot.C: Oxygen keeps hemoglobin in the **non-polymerizing** state
whyNot.D: Less 2,3-BPG **raises oxygen affinity**, keeping more HbS oxygenated and less able to polymerize

answer: Higher hemoglobin concentration inside the red cell (dehydration)
why: HbS polymerizes when **deoxygenated**, and the rate rises steeply with **hemoglobin concentration**, so dehydration increases sickling. Acidosis and low oxygen tension also promote it, while **HbF** and high oxygen tension protect.
chain: Dehydration concentrates hemoglobin inside red cells
Deoxy-HbS polymerizes faster
Red cells sickle and block small vessels in the feet (dactylitis)
Fetal hemoglobin and oxygen reduce sickling

idea.rule: Sickling rises with deoxygenation, acidosis and concentration; HbF protects.
also: Hydroxyurea raises HbF and reduces crises
Infants are protected until HbF falls after about 6 months
Renal medulla (hypoxic, acidic, hypertonic) favors sickling: papillary necrosis, even in trait
Hypoxia, infection and cold trigger crises
